name: Bangkok
tagline: Golden spires, river ferries and the best street food on earth
description:
Bangkok runs on contrast and appetite. Gilded temples and a royal palace crowd the old riverside district of Rattanakosin, while a few Skytrain stops away glass towers hold rooftop bars, vast air-conditioned malls and some of Asia's most inventive restaurants. Between them lies the real city: lanes of shophouses, noodle carts, spirit houses draped in marigolds and motorcycle taxis in orange vests.

Eating is the main event. You can spend a week grazing on boat noodles, grilled pork skewers and mango sticky rice for a few dollars a day, then splurge on a tasting menu that reinvents royal Thai cuisine. Chinatown's Yaowarat Road after dark is a pilgrimage in itself, all sizzling woks and flickering neon.

The heat is intense year-round, so plan temples for early morning, retreat to a gallery, mall or massage chair at midday and head back out when the air cools. Use the Chao Phraya river boats as much as you can; the river is faster than the traffic and far more scenic.

safety.notes: Bangkok is generally safe, but classic scams are everywhere: strangers claiming the Grand Palace is closed, tuk-tuk drivers steering you to gem shops, and unmetered taxis. Use Grab or insist on the meter, and watch your bag on crowded boats and in markets.

tipping: Tipping isn't obligatory, but leaving ฿20–50 at casual restaurants and ฿50–100 after a massage is customary, and upscale places add a 10% service charge.
gettingAround: The BTS Skytrain and MRT subway beat the traffic (the MRT accepts contactless bank cards), while Chao Phraya Express boats link the old town, Chinatown and Sathorn. Use Grab or Bolt instead of hailing street taxis.
tips: If a friendly stranger says the Grand Palace or a temple is 'closed today', smile and keep walking; it is the opening line of the infamous gem scam.
Ride the orange-flag Chao Phraya Express boat for a small flat fare instead of the pricier tourist boat; it stops at the same piers for Wat Pho, Wat Arun and Chinatown.
Download Grab or Bolt for fixed-price rides, and if you do take a street taxi, insist on the meter or walk away.
Street food runs on a timetable: rice porridge and fried dough sticks at dawn, curries over rice at lunch and the best grills and noodle stalls after 18:00.
Wear long trousers or a long skirt and carry a scarf for temples; the Grand Palace enforces its dress code strictly and sells cover-ups at the gate.
Most street stalls take a day off on Mondays for city cleaning, so plan your big street-food nights for other evenings.
etiquette: Never criticize or joke about the Thai monarchy; lèse-majesté laws are strictly enforced, and people stand for the royal anthem before films.
Don't touch anyone's head, and avoid pointing your feet at people, monks or Buddha images.
Women should not touch monks or hand items directly to them; place offerings on a cloth or ask a man to pass them on.
Remove your shoes before entering temple buildings and homes, and keep shoulders and knees covered at religious sites.

neighborhoods.name: Rattanakosin
neighborhoods.blurb: The historic royal district of the Grand Palace, Wat Pho and national museums, laced with canals and faded shophouses.

neighborhoods.name: Yaowarat (Chinatown)
neighborhoods.blurb: Neon-lit, gold-shop-lined Chinatown whose street-food scene explodes after sunset, with the hidden riverside alleys of Talat Noi next door.

neighborhoods.name: Sukhumvit
neighborhoods.blurb: The long, buzzing artery of international restaurants, rooftop bars, malls and nightlife, all strung along the BTS line.

neighborhoods.name: Ari
neighborhoods.blurb: A leafy, low-key residential quarter where Thai creatives hang out in indie cafés, noodle shops and craft beer bars.

neighborhoods.name: Silom
neighborhoods.blurb: Business district by day and nightlife hub by night, bordered by Lumphini Park and packed with rooftop bars and street stalls.

dishes.name: Tom yum goong
dishes.description: Hot-and-sour prawn soup sharp with lemongrass, galangal, lime and chili; the creamy version adds evaporated milk for extra richness.

dishes.name: Pad kra pao
dishes.description: Minced pork or chicken stir-fried with holy basil and bird's-eye chili, served over rice with a crispy fried egg; Bangkok's default lunch.

dishes.name: Boat noodles
dishes.description: Tiny, intensely rich bowls of beef or pork noodle soup thickened with spices and blood, once sold from canal boats; locals stack the empty bowls high.

dishes.name: Khao man gai
dishes.description: Poached chicken over rice cooked in chicken fat and garlic, with a punchy ginger-and-fermented-soybean sauce and a cup of clear broth.

dishes.name: Mango sticky rice
dishes.description: Ripe yellow mango with sweet, coconut-drenched glutinous rice and crunchy mung beans, at its peak from March to May.

events.name: Chinese New Year in Yaowarat
events.description: Chinatown turns red and gold with lion dances, firecrackers and food stalls as the city's large Thai-Chinese community welcomes the lunar new year; the date shifts between late January and February.

events.name: Songkran
events.description: Thai New Year (13–15 April) becomes a citywide water fight, with Silom Road and Khao San Road closed to traffic, while temples hold gentler merit-making rituals.

events.name: Vegetarian Festival
events.description: For nine days in the ninth lunar month, yellow flags mark stalls across Chinatown selling plant-based 'jay' food as devotees abstain from meat.

events.name: Loy Krathong
events.description: On the November full moon, people float candle-lit baskets of banana leaf and flowers on the Chao Phraya and park lakes to thank the water spirits.

attractions.name: Grand Palace
attractions.description: The former royal residence is a dazzling compound of gilded spires, mirrored mosaics and guardian giants, and it houses the Emerald Buddha in Wat Phra Kaew, Thailand's most sacred image. The ticket also covers a textile museum on site, a cool refuge worth a look.
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive at the 08:30 opening with shoulders and knees covered, and ignore anyone outside who says it is closed.

attractions.name: Wat Pho
attractions.description: Home to a 46-meter gold-leafed reclining Buddha whose feet are inlaid with mother-of-pearl, Wat Pho is also the birthplace of traditional Thai massage. Its quieter back courtyards hold rows of serene Buddha images and glittering tiled stupas.
attractions.bookingTip: Book a massage at the temple's own school after your visit; queues are shortest before 10:00.

attractions.name: Wat Arun
attractions.description: The Temple of Dawn's central spire, studded with broken Chinese porcelain in floral patterns, rises straight from the west bank of the Chao Phraya. Climb the steep lower terraces for river views, then cross back at sunset to see it glow from the opposite bank.
attractions.bookingTip: Take the short cross-river ferry from Tha Tien pier behind Wat Pho, and book a riverside rooftop table for the sunset view back across.

attractions.name: Chatuchak Weekend Market
attractions.description: With more than 15,000 stalls spread across 27 sections, this is one of the world's largest markets, selling everything from vintage denim and ceramics to houseplants and coconut ice cream. Grab a map near the clock tower and focus on a few sections, or you will wilt before lunch.
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive at 09:00 before the heat and crowds peak, and take the MRT to Kamphaeng Phet station, which exits right into the market.

attractions.name: Jim Thompson House
attractions.description: The American entrepreneur who revived Thailand's silk industry assembled six teak houses beside a canal and filled them with Asian art, before vanishing mysteriously in the Malaysian highlands in 1967. Guided tours tell the story, and the garden café makes a lovely pause.
attractions.bookingTip: English tours leave frequently throughout the day; book a slot online on busy weekends.

attractions.name: Lumphini Park
attractions.description: Bangkok's green lung is a 57-hectare oasis of lakes, jogging tracks and open-air aerobics classes, patrolled by surprisingly large monitor lizards. At 18:00 the national anthem plays over loudspeakers and the whole park freezes in place.
attractions.bookingTip: Come at dawn for tai chi groups or at dusk for the free group aerobics, and rent a swan pedal boat on the lake for a few dollars.

attractions.name: Yaowarat Road
attractions.description: Chinatown's main artery becomes one long open-air restaurant after sunset, as stalls fire up woks for oyster omelettes, fish maw soup and toasted buns with pandan custard beneath towering neon signs. By day, explore gold shops, herbal pharmacies and the narrow Sampeng Lane wholesale market.
attractions.hours: Street food roughly 17:00–midnight; many stalls closed Mon
attractions.bookingTip: Take the MRT to Wat Mangkon station and arrive hungry; queues at the famous stalls move faster than they look.

attractions.name: Mahanakhon SkyWalk
attractions.description: Perched on top of one of Thailand's tallest towers, more than 300 meters up, this observation deck has a glass-floored section that delivers vertigo on demand. Arrive before sunset, watch the city light up, and linger for a drink at the open-air rooftop bar.
attractions.bookingTip: Online tickets are cheaper than at the counter; pick a sunset slot and expect a short wait for the glass floor on busy nights.

attractions.name: Bangkok Art and Culture Centre
attractions.description: A white spiral atrium winds up through rotating exhibitions of Thai and Southeast Asian contemporary art, with indie bookshops and cafés on the lower floors. Entry is free and the air conditioning is ferocious, perfect for the hottest part of the day.
attractions.bookingTip: It connects directly to National Stadium BTS station, so pair it with the Jim Thompson House a short walk away.

attractions.name: Wat Saket
attractions.description: Better known as the Golden Mount, this temple crowns an artificial hill reached by more than 300 steps that wind past small waterfalls, bells and gongs. The gold stupa at the summit offers a 360-degree view over the old city's rooftops, glorious in late-afternoon light.
attractions.bookingTip: Ring the bells on the way up for luck, and visit in November when the temple fair fills the grounds with food stalls and rides.

hotels.name: Baan Mae Nam Residences
hotels.description: Restored teak mansions and a sleek new wing face Wat Arun from the Tha Tien bank, with a private boat shuttle to the city's riverside piers. The infinity pool and rooftop terrace have front-row seats for the Temple of Dawn at sunset.

hotels.name: Baan Khlong Lamphu
hotels.description: Three century-old shophouses converted into 18 rooms with terrazzo floors, four-poster beds and canal-view balconies. The Golden Mount is a five-minute walk, and breakfast brings rice soup and strong Thai coffee.

hotels.name: Sampeng Bunk House
hotels.description: A converted Chinatown warehouse with pod bunks, a rooftop hangout overlooking Yaowarat's neon and a free street-food walk every evening. Wat Mangkon MRT station is at the end of the lane.

hotels.name: Chang Silp Hotel
hotels.description: Each floor is curated by a different Thai artist, with rotating installations in the lobby and screen-printed textiles in the rooms. A skybridge links it to the BTS, and the rooftop pool gazes across the malls of Siam.

hotels.name: Lumphini Garden Suites
hotels.description: Spacious serviced apartments with full kitchens and washer-dryers overlooking the park's lakes, ideal for families and longer stays. Guests get free early-morning runs around the park with a trainer and a kids' pool on the seventh floor.

hotels.name: Chatuchak Garden Inn
hotels.description: A simple, spotless inn on a leafy lane between Ari's cafés and the weekend market, with a small garden and a free Thai breakfast. Rooms are compact but quiet, and the BTS is a seven-minute walk.

restaurants.name: Hoi Tod Mangkon
restaurants.description: A pavement stall where a husband-and-wife team fry crisp-edged oyster omelettes on a roaring flat-top beneath a buzzing neon sign. Grab a plastic stool, add a bowl of fish maw soup from the neighbor and douse everything in chili sauce.

restaurants.name: Phan Fa Boat Noodles
restaurants.description: A canal-side shop serving tiny bowls of rich, spiced beef or pork broth with rice noodles, pork crackling and morning glory for well under a dollar each. Regulars order five or six at a time and stack the empties as a badge of honor.
restaurants.signatureDish: Kuay teow reua (boat noodles) with beef

restaurants.name: Kafae Tha Tien
restaurants.description: A riverside shophouse café by the old Tha Tien pier market, serving old-style Thai drip coffee with fried dough sticks for dunking in pandan custard, plus eggs and toast. Grab a window seat facing Wat Arun.
restaurants.signatureDish: Kafae boran with pa thong ko and pandan custard

restaurants.name: Ton Phayom
restaurants.description: A twelve-course tasting menu that revives recipes from old Siamese court cookbooks, served in a hushed teak dining room high above Silom. Look out for river prawn with fermented rice and a green curry paste pounded at your table.
restaurants.signatureDish: Tableside-pounded green curry with dry-aged duck

restaurants.name: Bistro Soi Sarasin
restaurants.description: A candlelit French bistro facing the park, popular with embassy staff for steak frites, a proper cheese trolley and a fair wine list in a city where wine is heavily taxed. Weekend brunch spills onto the terrace.

restaurants.name: Jai Dee Isan Kitchen
restaurants.description: Sticky rice in woven baskets, charcoal-grilled chicken and pounded papaya salad made as fiery as you dare, served in a breezy open shophouse near the market's back gates. Great for a group after a morning of shopping.

restaurants.name: Baan Phak Wan
restaurants.description: A meat-free kitchen in a wooden house beside the Saen Saep canal, cooking pumpkin massaman, mushroom larb and banana-blossom salad without fish sauce or shrimp paste. Vegan dishes are clearly marked and the cooks will adjust the heat.

restaurants.name: Wang Luang Khao Gaeng
restaurants.description: An old-school curry shop a short walk from the palace, with around twenty trays of curries, stir-fries and relishes lined up out front. Point at two or three toppings and lunch comes to about $2.50.

experiences.name: Thonburi Canals Long-tail Boat Journey
experiences.description: Glide through the canals of Thonburi on a private long-tail boat, past stilt houses, temple piers where locals feed catfish and a family orchid nursery. Your guide stops for noodles served straight from a paddling vendor's boat.

experiences.name: Chinatown After Dark Street Food Crawl
experiences.description: Follow a Chinatown-born guide through ten tastings from smoky wok stalls, a century-old dessert shop and a hidden alley grill, while hearing how Teochew immigrants shaped Bangkok. Finish with a Thai craft beer in a restored shophouse bar.
includes: One craft beer or soft drink

experiences.name: Traditional Thai Massage Workshop
experiences.description: Learn the foundations of nuad thai in a small-group workshop led by teachers trained in the Wat Pho tradition, practicing stretches and pressure-point sequences on a partner. You leave with a certificate and moves to soothe sore travel legs.

experiences.name: Ayutthaya Ruins by Train and Bicycle
experiences.description: Take an early train north to the former royal capital of Ayutthaya, then cycle between crumbling towers, a Buddha head entwined in tree roots and riverside temples with an archaeologist guide. Lunch features the town's famous grilled river prawns.
